name: Apparent Temperature (Australian)
description: Estimates the felt apparent temperature using the Australian Bureau of Meteorology formula, adjusting air temperature upward for humidity through vapor pressure and downward for wind speed. It reflects how hot or cold the air actually feels.
notes: Air temperature is in Celsius, vapor pressure in hectopascals, and wind speed in meters per second. This shade formula excludes direct solar radiation, which would raise the felt temperature further.

name: Saturation Vapor Pressure over Ice (Magnus)
description: Computes the saturation vapor pressure over ice at a given temperature using the Magnus formula. The result gives the maximum water vapor pressure at which air is saturated with respect to an ice surface.
notes: Temperature is in Celsius and the ice-specific coefficients apply below freezing, near 0 to −65 °C. Vapor pressure over ice is lower than over liquid water at the same subzero temperature.

name: Wet-Bulb Temperature (Stull)
description: Estimates the wet-bulb temperature from air temperature and relative humidity using Stull's empirical fit. The wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature air can reach by evaporative cooling and indicates heat stress.
notes: Air temperature is in Celsius and relative humidity is a percentage from 0 to 100, not a fraction. The fit is accurate near standard sea-level pressure and loses accuracy at low humidity or high altitude.

name: Potential Temperature (Poisson)
description: Computes the potential temperature: the temperature a dry air parcel at temperature T and pressure p would reach if brought adiabatically to the reference pressure p0. Using Poisson's relation with exponent Rd/cp ≈ 0.286, it gives a temperature conserved during dry adiabatic motion.
notes: T must be absolute (kelvin); p0 and p share the same unit so their ratio is dimensionless. The 0.286 exponent applies to dry air; for moist or unsaturated conditions the exponent differs slightly.

name: Lifting Condensation Level (Espy)
description: Estimates the lifting condensation level height, the altitude at which a rising air parcel becomes saturated and cloud base forms. Espy's rule multiplies the surface temperature–dew point spread by 125 m per degree.
notes: T and Td are in °C and only their difference matters; the result is an approximation valid for typical near-surface conditions. A larger dew point depression means a higher, drier cloud base.

name: Clausius-Clapeyron Vapor Pressure
description: Calculates the saturation vapor pressure of water as a function of temperature using an integrated Clausius-Clapeyron form anchored at 273.15 K where es ≈ 6.112 hPa. Saturation pressure rises sharply, roughly doubling every 10 K.
notes: Temperature T must be in kelvin; the 5423 K coefficient assumes a constant latent heat, so accuracy degrades far from around 0–40 °C. Output is over a flat liquid water surface.

name: Hypsometric Equation (Thickness)
description: Computes the geopotential thickness of an atmospheric layer between two pressure levels using the hypsometric equation. The thickness is proportional to the mean virtual temperature Tv and the logarithm of the pressure ratio p1/p2.
notes: p1 is the lower (higher-pressure) level and p2 the upper level; their ratio is dimensionless so any consistent pressure unit works. Warmer mean layers are thicker. Tv must be in kelvin.

name: Virtual Temperature
description: Computes the virtual temperature, the temperature that dry air would need to have the same density as moist air at the same pressure. The moisture correction adds about 0.61 times the mixing ratio to account for water vapor being lighter than dry air.
notes: T is in kelvin and w is a mass mixing ratio in kg/kg (not a percentage); virtual temperature is always slightly higher than the actual temperature for humid air.

name: Geostrophic Wind Speed
description: Estimates the geostrophic wind speed from the balance between the horizontal pressure gradient and the Coriolis force. It divides the pressure difference dp over distance dn by the product of the Coriolis parameter f and air density rho.
notes: Use SI units: dp in pascals and dn in metres. The formula assumes straight, steady flow and breaks down near the equator where f approaches zero.

name: Precipitable Water (single layer)
description: Computes the precipitable water depth of a single atmospheric layer, the height of liquid water obtained if all vapor in the layer condensed. It integrates specific humidity q over the pressure thickness dp, divided by water density and gravity.
notes: Use SI units: dp in pascals gives a result in metres (multiply by 1000 for millimetres). q is specific humidity in kg/kg and assumed constant across the layer.

name: Radio Refractivity (N-units)
description: Computes atmospheric radio refractivity in N-units, the scaled excess of the refractive index over unity for radio waves. It sums a dry term proportional to pressure over temperature and a wet term proportional to vapor pressure over temperature squared.
notes: P and vapor pressure ev are in hPa and T in kelvin. The wet term dominates in humid air; N-units equal (n − 1) × 10^6.

name: Saturation Mixing Ratio
description: Computes the saturation mixing ratio, the mass of water vapor per unit mass of dry air when the air is saturated. It scales the saturation vapor pressure es by 0.622 (the water-to-dry-air molar mass ratio) divided by the partial pressure of dry air, p − es.
notes: es and p must share the same unit (hPa); the 0.622 factor is the ratio of molar masses. Result is in kg/kg, not a percentage.

name: Specific Humidity from Mixing Ratio
description: Converts the water vapor mixing ratio w (mass of vapor per mass of dry air) into specific humidity (mass of vapor per mass of total moist air) via w/(1+w). The two measures nearly coincide for small values.
notes: w is a dimensionless mass ratio in kg/kg; result is also kg/kg. For typical atmospheric values the difference from w is only about 1%.

name: Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate
description: Computes the dry adiabatic lapse rate, the rate at which an unsaturated air parcel cools as it rises, by dividing gravity g by the specific heat of air at constant pressure cp. With standard values it gives about 0.0098 K/m, or 9.8 K per kilometre.
notes: Result is in K/m; multiply by 1000 for the familiar ~9.8 K/km. Applies only to unsaturated (dry) parcels—once condensation begins the moist lapse rate is smaller.

name: Moist Adiabatic Lapse Rate
description: Computes the saturated (moist) adiabatic lapse rate, the cooling rate of a rising saturated air parcel, accounting for latent heat released by condensing water vapor. Because condensation warms the parcel, this rate is smaller than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
notes: Use SI units with T in kelvin and ws in kg/kg; the 0.622 factor is the molar mass ratio. The rate varies strongly with temperature and saturation mixing ratio.

name: Wind Profile Power Law
description: Estimates wind speed at a target height z from a known reference speed ur at reference height zr using the power-law wind profile. The ratio of heights is raised to the shear exponent alpha, which encodes surface roughness and stability.
notes: z and zr must use the same length unit; alpha is dimensionless (about 1/7 ≈ 0.143 over open terrain). The power law is empirical and less reliable in very stable or unstable conditions.

name: Logarithmic Wind Profile
description: Computes wind speed at height z in the neutral surface layer using the logarithmic wind profile. It multiplies the friction velocity ustar by the natural log of z over the roughness length z0, divided by the von Kármán constant.
notes: z and z0 use the same length unit and z must exceed z0. Valid for near-neutral atmospheric stability; wind speed is zero at height z0.

name: Beaufort Wind Speed
description: Converts a Beaufort force number B into an equivalent wind speed in m/s using the empirical relation 0.836·B^1.5. It approximates the mean 10 m wind speed corresponding to each Beaufort scale category.
notes: B is the integer Beaufort force (0–12); the formula is an empirical fit giving the representative, not exact, speed for each category.

name: Humidex
description: Computes the Canadian humidex, a perceived-temperature index combining air temperature with humidity. It adds to the air temperature a term derived from the water vapor pressure at the dew point, expressing how much hotter humid air feels.
notes: Air temperature T is in °C while the dew point Tdew is entered in kelvin here; the index is dimensionless and defined mainly for warm, humid conditions.

name: Total Totals Index
description: Computes the Total Totals stability index used to assess the potential for thunderstorms. It combines the 850 hPa temperature and dew point with twice the 500 hPa temperature; higher values indicate greater instability.
notes: All temperatures are in °C. As a rule of thumb, values above roughly 50 signal strong severe-storm potential; it is one of several composite indices.

name: Coriolis Force
description: Computes the magnitude of the Coriolis force on a mass m moving at velocity v on a rotating Earth. It equals 2·m·omega·v·sin(phi), so the deflecting force grows with latitude and vanishes at the equator.
notes: omega is Earth's angular velocity in rad/s and latitude phi must be in radians. This gives only the horizontal component magnitude for motion along the surface.

name: Brunt-Väisälä Frequency
description: Computes the Brunt-Väisälä (buoyancy) frequency, the angular frequency at which a vertically displaced air parcel oscillates in a stably stratified atmosphere. It is the square root of g times the vertical gradient of potential temperature divided by the reference potential temperature.
notes: theta must be in kelvin and dtheta/dz positive for stable stratification; a negative gradient makes the argument negative and the atmosphere unstable, so the square root is undefined.

name: Wind Chill Index (Canada)
description: Computes the Canadian wind chill index, the perceived temperature caused by wind removing body heat. It combines air temperature T with wind speed V raised to the 0.16 power in an empirical regression formula.
notes: T is in °C and V in km/h; the formula is valid for temperatures at or below 10 °C and winds above about 5 km/h.

name: Mixing Ratio from Vapor Pressure
description: Computes the water vapor mixing ratio, the mass of vapor per unit mass of dry air, from the actual vapor pressure ev and total pressure p. It multiplies the molar mass ratio 0.622 by ev divided by the dry-air partial pressure p − ev.
notes: ev and p must use the same unit (hPa); the result is in kg/kg. Uses actual vapor pressure, not saturation—use es to get the saturation mixing ratio instead.

name: Relative Humidity from Mixing Ratio
description: Computes relative humidity as the percentage ratio of the actual mixing ratio w to the saturation mixing ratio ws. It expresses how close the air is to saturation.
notes: w and ws must share the same unit (kg/kg); the result is a percentage. This mixing-ratio definition of RH differs slightly from the vapor-pressure definition.
